title: As the deer (Psalm 42)
hook: as a deer pants for water; why are you cast down, my soul?
carry: why so cast down, my soul?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm thirty-seven, for anyone lying awake replaying what someone else got away with. Your line was the meek shall inherit the earth. Did you set one grudge down, even for an hour? Day four hundred twenty-two.

The stream bed is mostly stones now. A deer comes down the hillside the way it always has, to the place where the water ran in spring, and stands there, sides heaving, nose low, searching. It knows exactly what it needs. It just can't find enough of it. Now set a person beside that deer. Someone who used to walk with the crowd on feast days, singing all the way up to the house of God, and who now lives far away, while the people around him ask, again and again, so where's your God now? Today's psalm opens with that deer. And then it does something unusual. The writer turns around and starts talking to his own soul.
screen: `A DRY STREAM BED.` → `A THIRSTY DEER.` → `A HOMESICK SINGER.`

segments.voice: Psalm forty-two begins, in the King James Bible: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God." A hart is an old English word for a male deer. The Hebrew for those brooks means channels of water, the kind that run full in the rainy season and can shrink to nothing in a dry one, so some readers picture an animal hunting for water that's hard to find. That is the feeling of the whole psalm. Its heading gives it to the sons of Korah, a family of temple singers. The writer remembers leading the crowds to the house of God with shouts of joy. Now he's far off, by the Jordan and the slopes of Mount Hermon, and he says: "My tears have been my meat day and night, while they continually say unto me, Where is thy God?" Meat, in older English, simply meant food. He has been living on tears. Then the turn. He speaks to himself. "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God." He asks his own sadness a question, and then gives it a gentle instruction. Not snap out of it. Hope. The same lines come back three times, twice here and once in Psalm forty-three, which is one reason some readers treat the two psalms as a single poem. And between the refrains, the sadness doesn't vanish: "Deep calleth unto deep," he says, every wave going over his head. In this psalm, thirst isn't a failure of faith. It's a measure of how much someone wants God.
screen: `A HART AT THE WATER BROOKS` · `TEARS FOR FOOD, DAY AND NIGHT` · `WHY ART THOU CAST DOWN, O MY SOUL?` · `THIRST IS A MEASURE OF WANTING` · then, large: `HOPE THOU IN GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak kindly to your own soul. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Notice what is low in you today. Tiredness, a worry, missing someone, a place you can't get back to. Don't push it away. Ask it the psalm's question, quietly, the way you'd ask a friend who looked down: why so cast down? Then listen. Whatever comes, answer it gently, without a lecture. If you pray, you can add the psalm's own words: hope thou in God. If you don't, just keep your soul company for a while. The bell holds the time.
As the deer. The opening of Psalm forty-two: a thirsty animal searching for water, and a person who misses God that much.
Your line: why so cast down, my soul? Today, when you hear yourself talking harshly to yourself, swap the lecture for the question. Ask it gently, and wait for an answer. Day four hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Psalm 42 in seasons of spiritual dryness, grief or homesickness; it is chanted in monastic daily prayer and sung in hymn versions such as "As pants the hart for cooling streams."

original.note: Hebrew: a deer, the hart of the King James Bible. Psalm 42 opens with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm picture of a deer by a stream.
what it means: a thirsty animal searching for water, and a homesick person talking honestly to their own sadness.
what a scholar hears: the refrain returns in 42:5, 42:11 and 43:5, one reason some readers treat Psalms 42 and 43 as a single poem.

notes: Editor review (y2 days 407–424): "walk at the front of the crowd" brought closer to 42:4 ("I went with them"); "many readers" and "many scholars" softened to "some readers" (the 42/43 single-poem view is now attributed, not stated as consensus, also in the myth and trapdoor); stock "the turn that makes this psalm so human" flattened; howItsDone "many" removed.
Hebrew 'afiqei mayim' (channels/streambeds of water): described as watercourses that can run low in a dry season; the dry-stream picture is offered as how many readers imagine it. Confirm phrasing.
Location from 42:6 ('the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites') given as 'by the Jordan and the slopes of Mount Hermon'. Confirm.
Refrain count: 42:5, 42:11, 43:5. The view that 42 and 43 were originally one poem is widespread (some Hebrew manuscripts join them); stated as 'many scholars think'.
howItsDone names the hymn 'As pants the hart for cooling streams' (Tate and Brady, New Version, 1696). Confirm attribution and wording of the first line.
